article.title: Reggio Emilia Stares Down an Uncertain Future
article.author: Giulia Lasagni
article.content: From early morning on August 3, around a hundred people placed themselves between machinery and 45,000 square meters of abandoned land on the eastern outskirts of Reggio Emilia, a northern Italian city about forty miles from Bologna. They came to prevent more than two hundred mature trees, dense undergrowth, and a pond from being cleared for a Conad supermarket. The project also included other planned buildings as well as parking, pavements, and bike lanes. The occupation, reached by a small road off the Via Emilia, quickly became a permanent encampment, with a field kitchen, tents, and nightly assemblies. About two months later, the area was cleared by police. The green space, now owned by the supermarket chain, was destroyed. The word bosco , woodland, was itself part of the battle. For developers, the site was abandoned land awaiting regeneration. For its defenders, the two decades of neglect had produced an urban forest that serves as badly needed green space in a city facing increasingly extreme weather. Bosco Ospizio poses the simple question of who really owns a site abandoned by both public authorities and private capital. Does it belong to the company that holds the deeds, to the city hall that approved its redevelopment, or to the people living with the consequences? The answer is controversial even locally. Many opposed the project and joined the campaign, while other residents supported redevelopment as a source of services, jobs, safety, and investment in an area they see as neglected. In Reggio Emilia, the question also carries unusual historical weight. The city was one of the great laboratories of Italy’s postwar Communist municipal left. For decades, the Emilia-Romagna region was celebrated for showing that Communists could govern democratically and effectively. Now it’s less clear that today’s left still has the same ability to resolve problems. The City as a Collective Project The “Emilian model” rested on strong municipalities, mass parties, trade unions, cooperatives, neighborhood organizations, and a dense associational culture. Political participation extended beyond elections through party branches, citizens’ committees, cultural associations, and negotiation between institutions and organized society. Urban planning was central. As postwar modernization transformed Emilia from an agricultural region into one of Europe’s most dynamic industrial economies, the Left faced the challenge of governing development, preventing speculation, and turning some of the newly generated wealth into public services. Planning meant deciding where people would live, how they would move, and which services they could access, regardless of income. The model shouldn’t be romanticized. It depended on party structures that were often hierarchical as well as participatory, and it treated economic growth as the central measure of success. Still, it also had a clear direction: public authority sought to shape the market and redistribute its gains. The city was understood as a collective political project. Bosco Ospizio points to an inversion of this relationship. The project was approved under a center-left mayor and carried forward by successive center-left administrations. In the Italian context, center-left refers to the convergence of different political traditions: not only the long-hegemonic Communist Party, but also the Catholic tradition of social reformism associated with Christian Democracy, particularly influential in Reggio Emilia through the legacy of Giuseppe Dossetti. In February 2026, city hall announced that building permits had been issued for the site. The proposal combines a 2,500-square-meter supermarket with a library, community hub, and health facilities, while retaining 23,000 square meters as public green space. This combination is the project’s strongest defense. Supporters see a practical compromise that would provide services, employment, and a safer, more accessible public space. Opponents argue that mature woodland, a pond, and established vegetation cannot be replaced by landscaping created after construction. “Public services are being delegated to a private entity,” one activist said. The problem is that the success of a commercial project here becomes the condition for obtaining collective infrastructure. The city hall may negotiate the details, grant permission, and promise mitigation measures, but it no longer commands the process; it only brokers it. Here as around Italy, local authorities have been squeezed for decades by fiscal restraint, privatization, and the erosion of their capacity to plan and invest directly. In this scenario, decisions about a neighborhood’s future migrate from the world of political programs and collective planning into business contracts, changes to urban planning, and negotiations with landowners. By the time residents ever get consulted, the fundamental choices may already have been made by others. “There had to be political will [for the Conad plan to go head],” this same activist said. Yet support for Bosco Ospizio shows that consultation cannot be dismissed as a mere exercise in managing dissent. The residents who support the project — prioritizing services, employment, safety, and the reuse of neglected land — surely do have a legitimate understanding of the public interest. For them, a library, health center, and supermarket may seem more valuable than preserving a site that was inaccessible or poorly maintained for years. The dispute is not simply, then, about whether Conad’s plan contains green space: it surely does. More than that, it raises the question of what kind of green space is needed, who defines its value, and whether the promised benefits justify destroying an existing ecosystem during a climate crisis. There is a further irony in this. For the supermarket Conad is not an alien multinational descending on a red city. Founded in Bologna in 1962 as a cooperative of independent retailers, the chain is still today organized through territorial cooperatives. While operating much like any other major supermarket chain, its cooperative origins point to a different economic and political tradition, one whose relationship with the territory has profoundly changed over time. It belongs, at least genealogically, to the same regional cooperative space that gave the Emilian model much of its rootedness in society. In this sense, too, the Bosco Ospizio is more widely revealing of the transformation of Emilia’s postwar institutions. The cooperative has itself become a major developer. The Communist municipality has become a center-left power broker. Citizens who once organized through mass politics now do so outside of such spaces, placing their bodies in front of construction machinery to reopen decisions that had formally been settled years earlier. Others accept or welcome the project as a practical response to local needs. In short, while the old institutions remain visible, the relationships involved in them have changed. A Mirror of the Left Today Bosco Ospizio is a small but unusually clear mirror of the Left’s wider predicament. For while center-left parties speak the language of equality, participation, and the ecological transition, their practice in government more often amounts to administering business as usual. This practice could easily be accused of hypocrisy. But more realistically, it is a reflection of a political model that prioritizes institutional competence over mass participation. As parties have retreated from workplaces and neighborhoods, their relationship with citizens has become thinner and more limited to election time. Political participation is only a fraction of what it once was. Public authorities, meanwhile, have lost resources, expertise, and confidence, becoming increasingly dependent on private actors to deliver investment. The Left may occupy the town hall, but it often lacks, or no longer tries to build, the social power needed to confront the interests shaping the city beyond it. If democratic participation cannot reopen a settled decision when ecological conditions, public priorities, and organized opinion have changed, then it becomes a kind of consultation without real consequences. And yet, if it ignores the residents who support the project, it also becomes exclusionary in a different way. The activists’ proposal to keep the green space revives a key feature of the Emilian tradition: planning as a democratic process while now updating that inheritance for a city that has been altered by the effects of climate change. The postwar left promised development with social protection. According to the Bosco activists, the Left today must recognize that existing nature is itself a form of essential infrastructure. We have said that the Emilian model ought not be romanticized. Its strength was not that the Communist mayors of old were exceptionally capable managers but lay in the fact that their administrations formed part of a larger attempt to shift power away from private wealth and toward organized citizens. This too is why Bosco Ospizio matters beyond Reggio Emilia. The idea of progressive municipalism is again in fashion today, from European cities confronting austerity to debates over what local government can and should do. The Emilian experience deserves attention in this regard, but not as a ready-made brand or as a success story worthy of nostalgia. At Bosco Ospizio, activists have forced these contradictions into the open. The battle over a patch of woodland has become a larger argument about what a city is for, whose needs count, and, ultimately, who gets to decide.
